metadata.description: Daily Reflection Tree - Three Axes of Growth

nodes.text: Good evening. Let's take a few minutes to reflect on your day. This isn't about judgment—it's about noticing patterns.
How would you describe today in one word?
options: Productive
Challenging
Frustrating
Rewarding
Overwhelming
answer=Productive|Rewarding:A1_Q_AGENCY_HIGH
answer=Challenging|Frustrating|Overwhelming:A1_Q_AGENCY_LOW

nodes.text: You said '{A1_OPEN.answer}'. When something went well today, what made it happen?
options: I prepared thoroughly and executed my plan
The team came through when it mattered
Things just aligned favorably
I adapted quickly when circumstances changed

nodes.text: You said '{A1_OPEN.answer}'. When things got difficult, what was your first instinct?
options: Identify what I could control and focus there
Wait for someone with more authority to step in
Push through it alone without asking for help
Feel stuck by circumstances beyond my control
answer=I prepared thoroughly and executed my plan|I adapted quickly when circumstances changed:A1_Q_CHOICE
answer=The team came through when it mattered|Things just aligned favorably:A1_Q_EXTERNAL_ATTR
answer=Identify what I could control and focus there|Push through it alone without asking for help:A1_Q_CHOICE
answer=Wait for someone with more authority to step in|Feel stuck by circumstances beyond my control:A1_Q_EXTERNAL_ATTR

nodes.text: Think about a specific moment today when you had to make a decision. What guided you?
options: My own judgment about what would work
What I thought others expected of me
Past experience with similar situations
I didn't feel like I had a real choice

nodes.text: When you think about what happened today, where do you see your influence?
options: In how I prepared and responded
In the relationships I've built over time
Honestly, not much—it was mostly external factors
In the small adjustments I made along the way
answer=My own judgment about what would work|Past experience with similar situations:A1_R_INTERNAL
answer=What I thought others expected of me|I didn't feel like I had a real choice:A1_R_EXTERNAL
answer=In how I prepared and responded|In the relationships I've built over time|In the small adjustments I made along the way:A1_R_INTERNAL
answer=Honestly, not much—it was mostly external factors:A1_R_EXTERNAL

nodes.text: You see your hand in what happened today. That's agency—not control over everything, but ownership of your response. Even when circumstances constrained you, you stayed in the driver's seat.

A difficult day pulls attention outward—to what others did or didn't do, to circumstances beyond your control. That's natural. But somewhere in there, you made choices. What were they? Even deciding to wait is a choice.
Now let's shift from how you handled things—to what you gave and what you expected.
Think about your interactions today. Which statement feels most true?
options: I helped someone with something outside my job description
I did my work well and expected recognition for it
I went out of my way to make someone else's day easier
I felt frustrated that my efforts weren't acknowledged
I taught someone something without being asked
answer=I helped someone with something outside my job description|I went out of my way to make someone else's day easier|I taught someone something without being asked:A2_Q_CONTRIBUTION
answer=I did my work well and expected recognition for it|I felt frustrated that my efforts weren't acknowledged:A2_Q_ENTITLEMENT

nodes.text: When you helped or contributed today, what motivated you?
options: It needed doing and I could do it
I wanted to be seen as helpful
It felt good to make a difference
I hoped they'd return the favor someday

nodes.text: When you think about what you deserved today, what comes to mind?
options: More recognition for the work I did
Better support from my team or manager
Nothing specific—I got what I earned
More resources or clearer direction
answer=It needed doing and I could do it|It felt good to make a difference:A2_Q_DISCRETIONARY
answer=I wanted to be seen as helpful|I hoped they'd return the favor someday:A2_Q_DISCRETIONARY
answer=Nothing specific—I got what I earned:A2_Q_DISCRETIONARY
answer=More recognition for the work I did|Better support from my team or manager|More resources or clearer direction:A2_Q_COMPARISON

nodes.text: Did you do anything today that wasn't required—something you chose to do?
options: Yes, I volunteered for something unglamorous
Yes, I improved a process without being asked
No, I stuck to my assigned responsibilities
No, I was too busy with required work

nodes.text: When you compare your effort to others on your team, how do you feel?
options: I give more than most and it's not always noticed
We all contribute differently—it balances out
Some people aren't pulling their weight
I focus on my own contribution, not comparisons
answer=Yes, I volunteered for something unglamorous|Yes, I improved a process without being asked:A2_R_CONTRIBUTION
answer=No, I stuck to my assigned responsibilities|No, I was too busy with required work:A2_R_TRANSACTIONAL
answer=We all contribute differently—it balances out|I focus on my own contribution, not comparisons:A2_R_CONTRIBUTION
answer=I give more than most and it's not always noticed|Some people aren't pulling their weight:A2_R_ENTITLEMENT

nodes.text: You're oriented toward giving. You did something today that wasn't required, wasn't tracked, and might not be noticed—and you did it anyway. That's organizational citizenship. It's also how trust gets built.

You're tracking what you're owed. That's not wrong—fairness matters. But entitlement becomes invisible to the person holding it. Ask yourself: if you got the recognition you wanted, would you give more? Or is the scorecard the point?

You stayed within the lines today—did what was required, no more. That's fair. But the space between 'required' and 'possible' is where growth happens. Not every day needs to be heroic. But some days could be.
Finally, let's zoom out. From 'what I did' to 'who it affected.'
When you think about today's biggest challenge, who comes to mind first?
options: Just me—it was my problem to solve
My immediate team—we were all affected
A specific colleague who had it harder than me
The customer or end user we're serving
The broader mission of what we're building
answer=Just me—it was my problem to solve:A3_Q_SELF
answer=My immediate team—we were all affected|A specific colleague who had it harder than me:A3_Q_TEAM
answer=The customer or end user we're serving|The broader mission of what we're building:A3_Q_TRANSCENDENT

nodes.text: When you were stressed today, what were you worried about?
options: My performance or how I'd be evaluated
Letting the team down
The impact on the project or customer
My own workload and capacity

nodes.text: You thought about others. Did you take any action based on that awareness?
options: Yes, I checked in with someone
Yes, I adjusted my work to help the team
No, but I noticed their situation
No, I was too focused on my own tasks

nodes.text: When you think about the end user or mission, how does that change your experience of today?
options: It makes the frustrations feel smaller
It reminds me why the work matters
It doesn't change much—I still had a hard day
It motivates me to push through obstacles
answer=My performance or how I'd be evaluated|My own workload and capacity:A3_R_SELF_CENTRIC
answer=Letting the team down|The impact on the project or customer:A3_R_TEAM_AWARE
answer=Yes, I checked in with someone|Yes, I adjusted my work to help the team:A3_R_ALTROCENTRIC
answer=No, but I noticed their situation|No, I was too focused on my own tasks:A3_R_TEAM_AWARE
answer=It makes the frustrations feel smaller|It reminds me why the work matters|It motivates me to push through obstacles:A3_R_ALTROCENTRIC
answer=It doesn't change much—I still had a hard day:A3_R_TEAM_AWARE

nodes.text: Today your frame was mostly self-referential—your stress, your performance, your workload. That's human. But self-focus amplifies pain. When you widen the lens to include others, problems don't disappear—they just take up less of the sky.

You're aware of others—you see the team, you notice when someone's struggling. That's perspective-taking. The next step is action: checking in, adjusting your work to help, making the team's success part of your own definition of a good day.

You're oriented outward. You think about the customer, the mission, the colleague who needs support. That's self-transcendence—Maslow's peak above self-actualization. It doesn't erase your own needs, but it contextualizes them within something larger. That's where meaning lives.
That's it. Same time tomorrow?

summary_templates.internal_contribution_altrocentric: You showed up with agency, gave without keeping score, and held others in your awareness. That's a day of growth. Not perfect—growth never is—but directionally sound.
summary_templates.internal_contribution_team: You owned your choices and contributed beyond what was required. You're aware of the team, even if you didn't always act on it. That awareness is the seed.
summary_templates.internal_contribution_self: You saw your agency and you gave. But your frame stayed narrow—focused on your own experience. Try this: tomorrow, when you're stressed, ask 'Who else is affected?' and see what shifts.
summary_templates.internal_entitlement_altrocentric: You see your hand in outcomes, but you're also tracking what you're owed. Interesting tension. The altrocentric lens helps—when you focus on the mission, the scorecard matters less.
summary_templates.internal_entitlement_team: You own your choices, but you're watching the scoreboard—who's giving, who's not, whether you're getting your due. Fair enough. But resentment is expensive. What would change if you stopped counting?
summary_templates.internal_entitlement_self: You see your agency, but you're focused on what you deserve and whether you're getting it. That's a narrow, exhausting frame. Try widening it: what did you give today that no one will notice?
summary_templates.internal_transactional_altrocentric: You own your responses and you think about the mission. But you stayed within the lines today—did what was required, no more. That's fine. Just know: the space between 'required' and 'possible' is where growth lives.
summary_templates.internal_transactional_team: You see your agency and you're aware of the team. But you played it safe today—stuck to your lane. Not wrong. Just limited. What would one discretionary act of help look like tomorrow?
summary_templates.internal_transactional_self: You owned your choices, did your job, and kept your focus narrow. Efficient. But also small. Growth requires stepping outside the transactional—giving something, noticing someone, widening the frame.
summary_templates.external_contribution_altrocentric: You gave today, and you thought about others. But you also felt constrained by circumstances beyond your control. Here's the thing: even when you can't control outcomes, you can control your response. That's where agency hides.
summary_templates.external_contribution_team: You contributed and you're aware of the team. But you attributed today's outcomes mostly to external forces. Ask yourself: where did you have a choice, even a small one? Agency starts there.
summary_templates.external_contribution_self: You gave something today, but your frame stayed narrow and externally focused—things happened to you. That's a tough combination. Try this: identify one decision you made today. Even deciding to wait is a choice.
summary_templates.external_entitlement_altrocentric: You felt constrained by circumstances and you're tracking what you're owed. But you also thought about the mission. That's a contradiction worth exploring. When you focus outward, does the scorecard matter less?
summary_templates.external_entitlement_team: You felt like today happened to you, and you're watching who's giving and who's not. That's a recipe for resentment. Try this: find one moment where you had a choice. Start there.
summary_templates.external_entitlement_self: Today felt like it happened to you, you're focused on what you're owed, and your frame stayed narrow. That's a hard place to be. Here's the way out: find one small thing you controlled. Then find another.
summary_templates.external_transactional_altrocentric: You felt constrained by circumstances, stayed within your job description, but thought about the mission. That's interesting. The mission is calling you toward something—maybe tomorrow you answer.
summary_templates.external_transactional_team: You felt like today happened to you, you stuck to your lane, and you're aware of the team. That's a starting point. Tomorrow: find one choice you made. Then make one discretionary contribution. See what shifts.
summary_templates.external_transactional_self: Today felt like it happened to you. You did what was required, no more. Your focus stayed on your own experience. That's the smallest possible frame. Here's the path out: agency first, then contribution, then widening your concern. One step at a time.
